Thomas Clarkson
tom'əs klärk'sən
n. (Thomas Clarkson, 1760–1846, English abolitionist, chief gatherer of evidence against the slave trade)
English patronymic Clark-son, son of the clerk.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Thomas Clarkson won a Cambridge Latin essay prize in 1785 on the question whether it is lawful to make men slaves against their will, and the research he did for it took over his life. He became the evidence-gatherer of the abolition movement, riding by his own count some thirty-five thousand miles through the ports of Bristol, Liverpool, and London, boarding ships, interviewing sailors, surgeons, and captains, and assembling the depositions on which the parliamentary case rested. He carried a chest of African manufactures — cloth, carved work, dyes, produce — to prove that the continent had trade to offer besides men, and he circulated the plan of the slave ship Brookes which showed the stowage to scale. Pro 31:8 is the commission he worked under, to “Open thy mouth for the dumb” (Pro 31:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a deposition as the testimony of a witness reduced to writing, and evidence as that which elucidates and enables the mind to see truth.

expand to see more

DEPOSI'TION, n. The act of giving testimony under oath; the attested written testimony of a witness.

EV'IDENCE, n. That which elucidates and enables the mind to see truth; proof arising from our own perceptions, or from the testimony of others.

TRAF'FIC, n. Trade; commerce, either by barter or by buying and selling; commodities of trade.

Key Scripture

Pro 31:8 — "Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction."

Isa 58:6 — "Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?"

Eph 5:11 — "And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them."

Psa 82:3 — "Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy."

Modern Corruption

Thirty-five thousand miles of interviews, a chest of African goods, and a ship's plan drawn to scale.

expand to see more

Clarkson's method is worth study by anyone who wants to see a wrong ended rather than deplored. He did not argue the principle, which Wilberforce argued in the House; he established the facts, in such volume and with such specificity that the trade's defenders could not maintain their account of it. Eph 5:11 commands not fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness “but rather reprove them” (Eph 5:11), and the Greek carries the sense of exposing to light, which is what a deposition does.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Pro 31:8 requires a voice for those who have none, and that supplying such a voice is mostly clerical labour: travel, note-taking, cross-checking, and years of it. Isa 58:6 names the end, to “let the oppressed go free” (Isa 58:6). Clarkson lived to see both the trade abolished in 1807 and slavery itself in the British empire in 1833, which few reformers of any cause are given.

Usage

"“Open thy mouth for the dumb” (Pro 31:8) — his commission for sixty years."

"“but rather reprove them” (Eph 5:11) — exposure to light, which is what evidence is."

"“let the oppressed go free” (Isa 58:6) — and he lived to see it twice."
